## 2

I'm curious: what specifically led you to that conclusion?

The reason the scientific consensus is so firm on the Earth being an oblate spheroid isn't just relying on modern space agencies—people proved the Earth was curved thousands of years before satellites or cameras existed. Ancient Greek thinkers like Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference with impressive accuracy simply by comparing the lengths of shadows in two different cities at the exact same time of day. 

Beyond historical measurements, there are everyday physical realities that only work on a globe: ships disappearing over the horizon hull-first, the curved shadow Earth casts across the Moon during every lunar eclipse, and the fact that observers in Australia see completely different constellations than observers in Canada. If every photograph, satellite feed, and space mission were faked, it would require a coordinated deception across millions of rival governments, independent scientists, pilots, and amateur astronomers spanning centuries. What model explains all of those natural phenomena better than a sphere?

## 3

To understand why the sky is blue, we first have to break down sunlight. Even though sunlight looks white, it’s actually a blend of all the colors of the rainbow combined together. You can see this happen whenever sunlight passes through a glass prism or raindrops, splitting into red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet.

Light travels as waves through space. Some colors, like red and orange, travel in long, lazy wavelengths. Other colors, like blue and violet, travel in short, quick, choppy wavelengths.

When sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with a thick blanket of gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. The long red and yellow waves pass right through these tiny molecules without bumping into much. But the short, choppy blue waves crash into the gas molecules and bounce off them in every direction. This scattering process is called Rayleigh scattering.

When you look up during the day, you aren't seeing straight-line sunlight; you're seeing all that blue light that was bounced around across the entire sky. 

(You might wonder: violet light has even shorter waves than blue, so why isn't the sky violet? Two reasons: the Sun naturally puts out much more blue light than violet, and the human eye is far more sensitive to blue than violet!)
